title: Dana Paramita
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of letting go of our limited individual selves to cultivate a sense of interconnectedness and generosity. By recognizing our inherent openness and receptivity, we can transcend feelings of "not enough-ness" and inadequacy, and instead discover the abundance and gifts that are always present in life. Through Zazen practice, we learn to allow things to arise and pass away without attachment or resistance, allowing us to receive life's gifts with an open heart and mind.

Is this in a good spot?
I can hear those words kind of reverberate through me: *An unsurpassed, complete and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.* It sounds like I have something special to offer you.
Yep, it's a little, I've never done a mic before.
It's kind of weird.
Okay, that sounds pretty good, huh?
So as those words reverberate through me, it sounds like I have something special here to offer to you.
But really, I have nothing special.
I have nothing that you don't already have within yourself.
So I'm sorry to say, I really have nothing to offer.
But thanks for being here anyway.
People ask me all the time, because I'm so recently ordained, so how does it feel to be a priest?
And I just don't know how to answer that question, because I don't want to disappoint them.
But really, again, it's nothing special.
I'm still myself, and I'm still practicing Zen.
So I ask myself then, well, has anything really changed?
I think my responsibilities have shifted.
I've settled more deeply into my vows, and in doing that, I'm given the opportunity to sit here and offer this dharma talk.
I also offer dharma classes.
But really, it's just my practice.
Just like you come to temple on Sunday morning, you sit.
Some of us sit together on weekday mornings on Zoom.
These are all an expression of our practice.
And as we move through our life, I know, as I've moved through my life, at different times my practice has taken different forms.
So right now, I'm practicing with this form of dharma study, offering dharma talks and dharma classes.
And it's still just my practice.
Nothing special.
Today, I'm going to talk about the first of the six paramitas, dana paramita.
If you come regularly on Sunday mornings, you'll see that the different practice leaders will have an opportunity to offer dharma talks on different Sundays.
And our loosely woven theme this year is the paramitas.
Dana paramita is considered the gateway, the entering gateway, to the bodhisattva path.
I see it as laying the groundwork for the other paramitas.
Why?
Because it requires a very fundamental shift in our attitude.
One of the most deeply conditioned attitudes we have is that of self-centeredness.
We learn early on: I am separate from you.
Mommy, me, daddy, sissy.
I can remember my children saying this as they individuated and learned this separateness.
And out of this naturally emerges a self-centered attitude.
If I exist as a separate entity, then I have to take care of myself.
I have to watch out for myself.

I have to attend to my needs and ensure that my needs are met: my needs for survival, for comfort, for pleasure, for growth, my need to be heard, my need to be accepted, my need to be loved, my need to be seen, my need to be understood.
And the list goes on and on and on, right?
We have a saying here in America: watch out for number one.
And in fact, we have a president who approaches international affairs with a put-America-first attitude.
It's the same mentality: watch out for number one.
Is this mic making too much extraneous sound?
Okay.
The thing is, it's not very tight on my head, so it moves around.
Can it tighten?
So, as I was saying, put America first.
It's the same mentality of watch out for number one.
This self-centered attitude, it's not just normalized, but it's deeply supported and culturally conditioned.
We learn it from a very early age.
The practice of dana, of generosity (I should have said this earlier, the translation of dana is generosity), confronts this learned separateness, this me-centered attitude.
Norman says in his book on the paramitas (maybe you've seen it, it's called *The World Could Be Otherwise*), he says, when we sit in the lap of the Buddha, there is no separate self.
So just close your eyes for a minute.
I want you to feel into this.
When you sit in the lap of the Buddha, there's no separate self.
What is it to sit in the lap of the Buddha?
Let's take a minute to breathe with that, to feel that.
What is it for you to sit in the lap of the Buddha?
Maybe it's to feel Buddha body.
My teacher refers to this as zazen body.
Sometimes I refer to it simply as presence, as being: that state of open, aware, and unencumbered by my ideas of how things should be, or my concepts, my concepts of how things are.

When we sit in the lap of the Buddha, for me, this also invokes the image of a child curled in his or her parent's lap, their parent's lap, feeling connected, feeling loved, feeling held by something bigger, a love that extends out to include the whole universe.
When we sit in the lap of the Buddha, there is no separate self.
We are a wave in the ocean of being.
And with this recognition, there is nothing to defend or to put first.
My life and your life are part of this endless web of interconnected being, of life that includes everything.
So how can I put myself first?
If my life is your life, how can I put myself first?
When we sit in the lap of the Buddha, we feel the inherent generosity of life, the endless gifts that life offers.
Have you noticed (and maybe you have, because everybody in this room sits zazen) that after each and every exhale, life offers you an inhale, no effort required?
You don't have to make it happen.
It happens.
This is an expression of life's inherent generosity.
It's the life that keeps on going.
And you can see it not just in your breath.
When you look around outside and you see how much cement we've laid over the earth, and yet in just a crack, the plants find their way up through the crack, expressing their aliveness.
We can cut open a body (a surgeon's job), even splitting open the sternum to perform open-heart surgery, and somehow again the body knows how to heal itself, so it can keep living.
What is it that enables us to recover from physical trauma such as that, from deep depression, from addiction, from trauma of terrible sorts?
I'm sure everybody in this room has either been through or witnessed some sort of either physical or emotional trauma, or maybe both.
And maybe you thought you weren't going to make it.
Maybe you thought you weren't going to come out the other side.
What got you through?
You're here.
You came out the other side.
Life miraculously keeps on giving.
When we're able to recognize the inherent generosity of life, there are always doors to open, always new possibilities, even when we've given up.
There are always ways to grow, and to grow and to learn and blossom.
Even in the hardest times, there is the potential to heal through most of life's challenges.

So cultivating dana paramita, the paramita of generosity, enables us to see life's gifts, and to recognize that sometimes our role is to simply get out of the way, and allow the inhale that naturally fills us when we exhale.
In Norman Fischer's chapter on dana paramita, in *The World Could Be Otherwise*, he writes, *Life itself is generous.
Life is always making more life.
Life is abundant and expansive, never stingy or small-minded.
It keeps on going, bubbling up and expanding wherever it has a chance.
You don't need to create life.
You just need to let it in.* I think this is the most important part.
You don't need to create life.
You just need to let it in.
And to do that, the practice of dana paramita is really about letting go.
Dogen calls this dropping body and mind: giving up self-clinging, that holding fast to the idea that I'm separate and I need to put myself first, I need to take care of myself first.
Letting go.
Easier said than done, right?
That's why we need practice.

Each time we sit down on our cushion, every time we invite ourselves back into this moment, just this, right here, right now, we're practicing letting go of what Okumura calls the limited individual self.
I quote him a lot.
The limited individual self.
I love his description of the conditioned self.
It feels so accurate to me.
Limited, yeah, implying disconnection from the life that keeps on giving.
A disconnected, bounded self, one that I must defend, that I must preserve.
Limited, and individual: the individual self implying that I'm separate, and that I'm small.
And in that smallness, I can feel a kind of deficiency.
I'm never enough.
I can't do good enough.
I can't be good enough.
I'm not smart enough.
I'm not pretty enough.
Just not enough.
Do you sometimes struggle with not-enough-ness?
I think it's an inherent part of being identified with the limited individual self.
This is the self that gets in the way.

Dogen's encouragement to drop body and mind: he's inviting us to let go of the limited sense of self, our identity with a limited self-concept, small-mindedness, and the self-centered disposition that is at the heart of this identity.
But the paradox is, of course, we can't try to let go.
As soon as we're trying, we're efforting in some way, which is, of course, the opposite of letting go.
It's something we need to learn to allow, like the next inhale.
If you can step aside, it will naturally happen.
And of course, this is why zazen practice is so helpful in cultivating dana paramita.
In zazen, we're practicing continually letting go.
When thoughts arise, we practice letting them float by, letting them come, letting them go.
When feelings or sensations arise, we practice letting them go, rather than indulging, hopping on the train.
We just let them come and let them go.
Zazen practice is, in itself, an expression of life's generosity.
Something bigger than the limited individual self brought you to practice, brings you to your cushion, and brings you to temple.
Have you ever thought about that?
What brought you here this morning?
Practice is like the breath that breathes you.
Just as the breath itself breathes life into you, practice too breathes life into you.
It breathes the life of compassion, of wisdom, of equanimity, of acceptance, to name just a few examples of how practice supports our growth, unfoldment, and the blossoming of our life.
We show up and then get out of the way.
And practice will show us the inherent abundance of being, the endless gifts that life bestows.
When we sit in the lap of the Buddha, we see that even in the difficult moments, right in the middle of life's challenges, even those challenges that seem insurmountable, these too are gifts.
Life is awakening.
I think this is Dogen's idea of continuous practice.
Everything we do is in service of awakening.
We can't help it.
It's unstoppable.
It's the inhale that most naturally and absolutely effortlessly follows the exhale, the letting go.
I remember when I started as shuso, all new shusos are invited to give a way-seeking mind talk.
And that was not so easy for me.
My life story had a lot of sadness in it.
I was a sad and lonely child.
I had a depressed and unresponsive mother.
And my own early adult years were characterized by my own struggles with depression.
Over the period of time when I wrote my talk (and I really took my time with that talk), I could feel emerging in me the sense that, even with its challenges, my life was perfect.
It couldn't be any other way, because it brought me to this day, and it made me who I am.
I wouldn't be sitting here with you today, on this Sunday morning at [unclear: "San Swede"] temple, if it weren't for each and every single thing that has happened in my life.
That was one of the first times that my experience of life as a gift really opened up.
So I invite you to pay attention.
Everything is saying, wake up, wake up.
If we get out of the way, everything is an expression of life's blossoming.
And when we really know that, we know the paramita of dana, generosity.
When Nomon Tim introduced the paramitas two weeks ago, letting everyone know that this was our theme, he described paramita as going beyond.
I love that.
I think he was talking about going beyond this limited, individual, self-centered self.
It's not me giving to you, because ultimately there's no me, there's no you.
We are all part of life's continuous flow of giving.

As we say in the meal chant, *may we, with all beings, realize the emptiness of the three wheels: giver, receiver and gift.* Norman really helped me make friends with that word emptiness when he said, [unclear: "it sure can for an empty sense of self"].
*We, with all beings, realize the emptiness of the three wheels: giver, receiver and gift.*

I was going to end my talk with that, but this morning, when we were chanting, something popped out at me that I just wanted to bring our attention back to, because it's relevant to what I'm talking about here.
I just have to find the page of the [unclear: "Genjokoansan 24"].

This is the third line of the Genjokoan, and I've heard it translated differently, but this translation stood out to me this morning: *The Buddha way is in essence leaping clear of abundance and lack, neither one or both.* So we have a little time, not as much as I hoped.
I wanted to go into dyads and
*[The recording ends here, partway through the talk.]*
